full_query: A 44-year-old homeless man presents to the emergency department after being stabbed multiple times in the abdomen. The patient is intoxicated and is unable to offer further history. His temperature is 97.5°F (36.4°C), blood pressure is 92/52 mmHg, pulse is 145/min, respirations are 33/min, and oxygen saturation is 90% on room air. He is intubated to protect his airway, given 2 units of packed red blood cells, and sent to the operating room for an exploratory laparotomy. The patient is subsequently admitted to the intensive care unit. He is extubated the next day and appears well. His vitals are within normal limits. Physical exam reveals sparse hair that is falling out throughout the patient’s body. He has a rash by the corners of his mouth. The patient has multiple loose bowel movements and on day 6 the patient’s surgical wound does not appear to be healing. It is held together only by the sutures with minimal underlying healing. Which of the following is most likely deficient in this patient? (A) Riboflavin (B) Thiamine (C) Vitamin C (D) Vitamin D (E) Zinc

sentences: To address the clinical query, we'll follow a step-by-step approach to identify the most likely deficiency in the patient
A 44-year-old homeless man presents with multiple stab wounds in the abdomen
Vital signs indicate hypovolemic shock: low blood pressure (92/52 mmHg), high pulse (145/min), and high respirations (33/min)
The patient is intoxicated, suggesting potential chronic alcohol use
Intubation for airway protection
Administration of 2 units of packed red blood cells
Exploratory laparotomy performed
Extubated the next day with normalized vital signs
Sparse, falling hair
Rash at the corners of the mouth
Multiple loose bowel movements
Poor wound healing by day 6 post-surgery
Sparse Hair and Rash: These symptoms suggest possible nutrient deficiencies
Loose Bowel Movements: This can be a sign of malabsorption or another underlying condition affecting nutrient absorption
Poor Wound Healing: Indicates a possible deficiency in nutrients essential for tissue repair

Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) Deficiency: Can cause sore throat, redness and swelling of the lining of the mouth and throat, cracks or sores on the outsides of the lips (cheilitis) and at the corners of the mouth (angular stomatitis)
Thiamine (Vitamin B1) Deficiency: Commonly associated with chronic alcohol use
Symptoms include beriberi, Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, but not typically hair loss or poor wound healing
Vitamin C Deficiency: Known as scurvy, presents with poor wound healing, perifollicular hemorrhages, and gingival disease
Hair loss and rash (especially around the mouth) can also be present
Vitamin D Deficiency: Mainly affects bone health, causing rickets or osteomalacia, and is less associated with hair loss or wound healing directly
Zinc Deficiency: Symptoms include alopecia (hair loss), dermatitis (especially around body orifices), diarrhea, and impaired wound healing
The combination of alopecia, rash at the corners of the mouth, diarrhea, and poor wound healing is most consistent with Zinc deficiency
(E) Zinc
